title: What Berlin Said When the 6th Army Stopped Responding from Stalingrad
fullText: February 2nd, 1943. 9:20. In a concrete bunker somewhere in the ruins of the Stalingrad tractor factory [music] district, a radio operator transmits. The signal is weak. The batteries are nearly spent. The words going out across the frequency are these. The Russians are penetrating. [music] Then nothing. The frequency holds open. A channel with nothing left to send. For months, Berlin had been talking to Stalinrad, [music] issuing orders, promising relief, sending promotions, speaking in [music] the language of destiny and sacrifice and the salvation of the Western world. And from the pocket [music] along the vulgar, broken and starving, a different language [music] had been coming back. The language of frostbite and dissentry, of 18,000 wounded without dressings, of a command structure that no longer commands anything. Now the pocket is silent. What did Berlin say when Stalingrad stopped responding? 6 months earlier, a thousand miles to the northwest, the summer of 1942, and a city on the Vular. Stalingrad stretched 30 mi along the western bank of the river. It was an industrial city, factory complexes, armament works, tractor plants converted for war production. Capturing it would sever Soviet supply lines running north to south through the interior and anchor the northern flank of the broader German drive toward the Caucus' oil fields. But there was something beyond strategy. The city bore the name of the Soviet leader. For Hitler, that alone made it personal. In the summer of 1942, General Friedrich Powus advanced on the city with 250,000 men, 500 tanks, 7,000 guns and mortars, and 25,000 horses. By October, German forces had pushed Soviet defenders to a narrow strip of rubble at the edge of the Vular. The city was almost gone. Then came November. On November 19th, the Red Army launched Operation Uranus, a two-pronged attack aimed not at the city itself, but at the thinly stretched Romanian armies, protecting the Sixth Army's flanks. The Romanians broke. Within 4 days, Soviet armored columns had swept around both sides of the German position. By November 23rd, at Kalak on the dawn, the encirclement was complete. Inside the ring, the Sixth Army and elements of the fourth Panzer Army, approximately 220,000 men, a pocket 35 mi wide and 20 m north to south. Field Marshal von Mannstein launched a relief operation in December, Operation Winter [music] Storm. Soviet resistance stopped it roughly 30 mi short of the pocket. Then a Soviet offensive, Operation [music] Little Saturn, smashed through Italian and Hungarian lines further west, threatening to encircle the relief force itself. Mannstein [music] fell back. The Sixth Army had no more hope of rescue from outside. There remained one lifeline, the air. [clears throat] And here is where the arithmetic becomes important. Because the arithmetic was fatal [music] before a single supply flight departed. Guring told Hitler his Luftvafa could deliver 300 tons of supplies daily. The Sixth Army [music] needed 750 to survive. The airlift across a winter of fog [music] and Soviet fighters and inadequate aircraft averaged approximately 105 tons per day. Hitler's standfast order, the order that condemned 220,000 men to hold a dying pocket through a Soviet winter, rested on a [music] number that could not survive contact with a pencil. The men in the pocket would be hungry. They would get hungrier [music] and they would understand long before the generals admitted it that the planes were not coming. Berlin was not reporting events. It was prescribing them. through October, [music] November, December. As the pocket compressed, [music] as the temperature fell, as typhus and dissentry spread through men whose immune systems had been stripped [music] bare by cold and starvation, the OKW communicates spoke of defensive fighting, of positions held, of the Eastern Front stabilizing [music] for renewed summer offensives. On November 8th, at the annual celebration of the Munich [music] beer hall push, Hitler addressed his most faithful audience and declared victory at Stalingrad. The city was not yet taken. The trap had [music] not yet fully closed. 18,000 men would later lie in that pocket without dressings or drugs, but the story of [music] triumph had already been given its premiere. The gap between the language and the terrain was [music] not carelessness. It was architecture. Joseph Gerbles understood that Stalingrad could not be framed as a triumph, [music] but it could be framed as something else entirely. The vocabulary shifted through the weeks. Sacrifice, fate, heroic endurance. [music] The German public began to hear a story about men dying for something. [music] The precise nature of what they were dying for was not part of the vocabulary. By late January, [music] the press ran headlines that openly strained plausibility. On January [music] 29th, all Soviet mass attacks repelled. The subtitle acknowledged that the defenders of Stalingrad [music] faced multiple enemy superiority. Attentive readers understood [music] something was badly wrong. They did not yet know how wrong. What flowed into the pocket [music] down those radio frequencies was a mirror image of what flowed out. The men in the pocket [music] spoke in specifics. Numbers, conditions, the names of what they lacked. Berlin spoke in myth. Two languages crossing the same wire. Only one of them connected to the ground. January 8th, 1943. A Soviet [music] envoy party approaches the German lines under a flag of truce. A major, a captain, and a trumpeter. They carry a letter signed by Colonel General Voronov and the commander of the Dawnfront, [music] Lieutenant General Roosovski. The terms are generous. Safety for all prisoners, medical care for the sick and wounded, personal belongings retained, repatriation after the war. Rokosovski's letter is direct about the [music] situation. The pocket is surrounded. Relief is impossible. Further resistance costs only lives. Powus transmits the offer to Berlin and requests permission [music] to accept. Hitler rejects it out of hand. On January 10th, the Soviet assault on the pocket begins. Nearly 7,000 field guns, launchers, and mortars opening simultaneously. the single largest artillery bombardment of the war to that point. The ring [music] begins to close. Pomnic airfield falls on January 16th [music] with Pomnik goes the only substantial landing strip in the pocket. The point [music] through which the wounded had been evacuated, through which supplies had arrived [music] in what quantities they did. The men who can no longer be flown out will not leave. Gumrak [music] falls on the night of January 21st. The third runway at the Stalin Gradskaya Flight School sees its last landings and takeoffs on January 23rd. After that, [music] there are no more aircraft landing in the pocket. There are occasional air drops, [music] bundles falling into the snow, sometimes inside German lines, sometimes outside them. That is all. January 22nd. Roosovski offers [music] terms again. Powus requests permission again. Hitler replies that same [music] day. The Sixth Army has made a historic contribution to the greatest struggle in German history. It will stand fast [music] to the last soldier and the last bullet. He has told Gerbles that the plight of the army is, in his words, a [music] heroic drama of German history. Then comes January 24th. Powerless transmits. Troops without ammunition or food. Effective command no longer possible. 18,000 wounded without any supplies or dressings or [music] drugs. Further defense senseless. Collapse inevitable. Army requests immediate permission to surrender in order to save lives of remaining troops. And Hitler's reply, surrender is [music] forbidden. Sixth Army will hold their positions to the last man [music] and the last round and by their heroic endurance will make an unforgettable contribution toward [music] the establishment of a defensive front and the salvation of the Western world. 18,000 wounded men without dressings. The salvation of the Western world. Military historians [music] would later calculate one dimension of this exchange that the men in the pocket did not know. Their [music] continued resistance through January was buying time for Army Group A, General Von [clears throat and music] Kle's forces to withdraw from the Caucuses. Had Powus [music] surrendered 3 weeks earlier when the Soviet terms were still on the table, Kle's escape would have been impossible. [music] The men dying in the snow were serving a real strategic purpose. But the purpose they were [music] being told they were dying for the salvation of the Western world was not that purpose. No one told them the difference. On January 26th, Soviet forces split the pocket in two. Powus [music] loses telephone communication with the northern mass of the army. The Sixth Army is no longer one thing. It is dissolving into core, into divisions, into regiments, then into smaller and smaller units making their own solitary calculations about what comes next. [music] The 76th Infantry Division, which entered the battle 10,000 men strong, is now 600. January 30th, 1943, the 10th anniversary of Hitler's seizure of power. By now, Powus has been living in [music] a basement. The command post of the Sixth Army's Southern Pocket is the basement of the Univer Department Store in central Stalingrad. Filthy, candle lit, stinking of unwashed bodies and illness. An accordion lies on a couch. [music] A candle end burns on the table. Powus himself lies on an iron cot in his shirt sleeves, too ill to maintain the appearance of command. His face [music] carries a nervous tick he cannot control. His stomach churns with dissentry. He is 6'4 in tall and he has been reduced [music] to borrowing a hat, gray rabbit fur, because the energy required to maintain the forms he once kept [music] has left him. The man who insisted on personal cleanliness on the worst battlefields of Europe is lying on a cot by candle light in a building that reeks. into this basement. Two things arrive [music] on January 30th. The first is a radio broadcast. Goring's voice from Berlin describing [music] Stalingrad as a mighty monument, one that one day will be recognized [music] as the greatest battle in our history. The men listening understand [music] what this is, an epitap written while they are still alive to hear it. The second is a transmission from Hitler. Powus [music] has been promoted. He is now a General Feld Marshall, a field marshal of Germany. The tradition of German arms held one unbroken precedent. No Prussian or German Field Marshall had ever surrendered. Not in the Wars of Bismar, not in the Francoressussian War. Not in four years of the last world war. The rank [music] carried an implicit obligation, a script written not in orders, but in precedent. Hitler was not giving Powus a reward. He was transmitting instructions [music] encoded in tradition concerning how this should end. A field marshall's baton [music] sent by radio to a man lying in his shirt sleeves on an iron cot surrounded on all sides with an accordion on a couch and a candle burning down. Palace understood the [music] subtext. Later in Soviet captivity, he would put it in plain language. He had no intention of shooting himself [music] for this bohemian corporal. He chose to live. Morning January 31st. Soviet troops of the 64th Army's 38th motorized rifle brigade [music] close on the uniform store. Soviet Lieutenant Ilchenko, among [music] the first to enter, finds Powus lying on that iron cot without a uniform in just his [music] shirt sleeves. The candle end on the table, the accordion on the couch, a face twitching with a tick, pale with illness. The man [music] sits up but does not stand. Ilchenko would write later that he had the [music] appearance of someone sick and physically exhausted. Before the Soviet officers arrive, Powus [music] transmits a final message. The Sixth Army, true to their [music] oath and conscious of the lofty importance of their mission, have held their position to the [music] last man. Then silence from the south. The surrender negotiations are conducted not by Powus, but [music] by his chief of staff, General Arthur Schmidt. short, stocky, and looking war [music] correspondents would note. Like a man who had not missed too many meals during the siege, Powus refuses to participate [music] directly. He will claim later to have been taken by surprise. The southern pocket is gone. But in the north, across the rubble and ice and the bodies frozen in the streets, General Carl Streker holds. Pow! Declines [music] to order him to surrender. Since January 30th, Streker's 11th core answers directly [music] to Hitler, not to Pow! Streker holds his own orders. The Soviet forces [music] concentrate everything on the northern pocket now. Artillery reduces [music] strong points. Tanks move to close range, firing directly into bunkers. The systematic [music] elimination of what remains. At 4 in the morning on February [music] 2nd, Streker receives word that one of his own officers has gone to the Soviets to negotiate [music] terms. He drafts his final transmission to Army Group Dawn. At 8:00, [music] the 11th Army Corps, consisting of six divisions, has fulfilled its duty by the heaviest fighting [music] to the very last. Hail to the Furer. Hail to Germany. Then at 9:20, [music] a final fragment picks up on the frequency. The Russians are penetrating. The signal ends mids sentence. No period, no sign off, no last word. The frequency holds open after the 8:00 signal was sent. After the formal compliance [music] had been transmitted, the furer's name still intact, Streker and his chief of staff, [music] Helmouth Gkgirth, drafted one more message. Those who received it noted afterward what was different. The furer's [music] name was gone. Replaced by two words. Long live Germany. Not the war. Not the Reich. Not the figure whose promotion had been transmitted [music] to the basement below 2 days earlier. Germany. A deliberate substitution sent into the ether as Soviet troops came through the last walls of the last German position in Stalingrad. The radio falls silent. February 3rd, 1943. The German public is told. The radio broadcast that morning describes men who had been overcome by the superiority of the enemy and by the unfavorable circumstances confronting the army. It names Paulus. It [music] speaks of exemplary leadership. It speaks of the oath they fought under. It does not say that [music] 91,000 German soldiers, including their field marshal, are alive and in Soviet custody. Three days of national mourning [music] are declared. Theaters close. Music plays, grave [music] ceremonial. The German public understands that something catastrophic has occurred. They understand [music] it as a death. They do not understand it as a surrender. The language does not permit them to. The broadcast, however, is not the most revealing thing Berlin said. That record comes from the Furer's headquarters on February 1st. Hitler speaks [music] to his staff. He is not grieving. He is not mourning the men who died in the pocket or the [music] 90,000 who did not. He is furious at one man. So many people [music] have to die, and then a man like that bismerches the heroism of so many others at the last minute. He could have freed himself from all sorrow and ascended into eternity and national immortality, but he prefers to go to Moscow. And then that's the last field marshal I shall appoint in this war. He appointed seven more before the war ended. The rage delivered at length to his assembled staff was not a man confronting a military [music] catastrophe. It was a man whose narrative had been refused by a single individual. The story required a field marshal who died in [music] the ruins. It received a field marshal who had shaved, put on a borrowed coat, [music] and introduced himself to a Soviet left tenant in broken Russian. Hitler had sent the ending he wanted down a radio wire. Palace had declined to perform it. 16 days pass. February 18th. The Sport Palast. The Berlin Sports Palace holds 14,000 and Gerbles fills it carefully, not with random Berliners dragged in from the street with party officials, war veterans, [music] workers, women. A curated assembly selected precisely for the responses they [music] can be counted on to deliver. He places the wounded in the front rows deliberately. Men in bandages, [music] men on crutches, men whose arms or legs are gone, men blinded in action, accompanied [music] by their nurses. The amputees sit at the front so the cameras [music] can find them and so Gerbles can gesture toward them when he needs proof. He opens by invoking the radio. He tells the [music] crowd something that stops just short of being true. The last heroic fighters in Stalingrad, [music] he says, heard the Furer's proclamation by radio and for perhaps the last time in their lives raised their hands to sing the national anthems. The last transmission from Stalinrad [music] came at 9:20 on February 2nd. The men Gerbles describes as raising their hands in a Nazi [music] salute were already in captivity or dead or dying in the snow. The radio [music] link he invokes did not exist. The silence which his machinery [music] had spent 16 days filling is recast in a single sentence into a gesture of devotion. The dead reaching across the ether to join the living in the sport palast saluting. He builds the speech toward its climax through 10 [music] questions. Each one louder than the last. Each one feeding the crowd's noise back into itself. Do you want total war? Do you want it more [music] total and radical than anything we can even imagine today? Are you resolved to follow the furer through thick [music] and thin to victory? The crowd surges to its feet. Fur command we will follow. His last line. Now people rise up and let the storm break loose. Albert Shpar watching from nearby would write that he had never seen an audience so effectively roused to fanaticism except at [music] Hitler's most successful public meetings. He described Gerbles afterward dissecting [music] the crowd's response not like a statesman who had moved his people but like an experienced actor running his notes after a performance. There is one [music] more detail. The audio recording of the sport palast rally survives and the crowd's response that unanimous roaring thunder that appears in the written transcript is in the recording at moments something less. The ovations [music] the transcript renders as absolute. The recording renders as somewhat less [music] orchestrated, somewhat less unanimous. The most famous expression of German popular fanaticism in the aftermath of Stalingrad was staged [music] in a hall filled by hand. And even that audience on occasion hesitated before it cheered. Of the 91,000 men taken prisoner in the frozen rubble around Stalingrad, approximately 5,000 made it home. The rest died not in battle but in captivity from the same forces that had been killing them in the pocket disease cold exhaustion [music] starvation. The men Berlin had called heroes died [music] anyway. More slowly in obscurity. Their deaths were not recorded as sacrifice. They were processed as statistics when they were processed at all. Friedrich Pow [music] outlived his wife. Elena had died in 1949. The last time he had seen her was late 1942 [music] before the ring closed. He moved to Dresden, worked in military [music] history research, and lived alone. His family imprisoned by Hitler in retaliation for his anti-Nazi broadcasts from captivity. [music] His name a symbol of either defeat or survival, depending on who was using it. He died on February [music] 1st, 1957. One day short of the 14th anniversary of the surrender he had agonized [music] over, his son Ernst died in 1970 at the age of 52, the same age his father had been [music] in that basement. 3 weeks after Germany learned the truth of Stalingrad, the carefully managed truth of it, [music] the version that still concealed the surrender, a pamphlet circulated in Munich. The White Rose, a small group of students and their [music] philosophy professor, Curt Huber, had been producing anti-Nazi leaflets [music] for months. Their sixth and final pamphlet opened. Devastated, our nation stands before the downfall [music] of the men of Stalingrad. The words were hubers. He denounced [music] the World War Lance Corporal's ingenious strategy that had driven 330,000 German men [music] to destruction without reason or responsibility. The Gestapo came. Sophie Schaw, Hans Schaw, Curt Huber, Alexander Schmorel, Billy Graph, Kristoff Props tried before the people's court under Roland Frysler who screamed at them from the bench. Then the guillotine. Three weeks between the silence and their deaths. Stalinrad's silence gave them the courage to [music] speak. The regime that manufactured the silence killed them for it. And then at the end, there is the frequency again. Not the official signal. Streker's 8:00 transmission with the furer's name still in it. The last act of formal compliance. Not Powus's final message about [music] oaths and missions. Not the incomplete fragment mid-sentence still hanging in the air like [music] a question no one came back to answer. The last deliberate transmission from Stalinrad. After the formal signals were sent, [music] after the Soviet troops were already coming through the walls, Streker and his chief of staff drafted one final message. They removed the Furer's name. They replaced it with something else. Two words addressed [music] to no one in particular, carrying no request and expecting no reply. Long live Germany. Not the war. Not the myth. Not the story Gerbles had spent [music] 16 days constructing before a hand selected crowd. Germany, the country stripped of the performance [music] built around it. sent into the ether as the last signal out of Stalenrad by a general who chose in the final moment available to him what to say [music] and what to leave out. Whether Berlin heard it is not recorded.
